Then, when He, exalted is He, said ﴿the knocker﴾, this was something whose hearer cannot do without knowing its intended meaning, so He said ﴿And what will make you know what the knocker is?﴾. Sufyān ibn 'Uyayna said: "Everything in the Qur'an introduced by 'what will make you know' (mā adrāka), the Messenger has informed about it; and everything in it introduced by 'what will make you know' (mā yudrīka) he has not informed about, such as His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Then He said ﴿the piercing star﴾, meaning: it is a knocker of great affair and high rank, and it is the star by which one is guided in the darknesses of land and sea, and by which the times of rains are determined. One: it pierces the darkness with its light, so it penetrates it, as it is said: "durrī" (a pearl-like star), because it repels (yadra'uhu) it, that is, pushes it away.

Two: it rises from the east penetrating the air, like something that pierces a thing.

Three: it is the one by which the devil is seen, so it pierces him, that is, penetrates him and burns him.

Four: al-Farrā' said: "the piercing star" is the star that is elevated above the stars. The Arabs say of a bird when it rises high into the belly of the sky: "it has pierced (qad thaqaba)."

**Second issue:** The star was described as a knocker because it appears at night, and you know that this is called ṭāriq; or because it knocks (yaṣukku) the jinn, that is, strikes them.

**Third issue:** Scholars differed concerning His saying ﴿the piercing star﴾. Some said: it refers to the group of grammarians, and it was said "the knocker," as it was said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [Al-'Asr: 2]. Others said: it is a specific star. Others said: it is the meteors with which the devils are stoned, because of His saying: ﴿So a piercing meteor pursued him﴾ [As-Saffat: 10].

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the thing sworn by, He followed it with mention of the thing sworn to: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian.﴾ Concerning this there are issues:

**First issue:** Concerning His saying "(lammā)" there are two readings:

One of them is this, and the other is in the matter of oaths: you say, 'I asked you by Allah, lammā you did such-and-such,' meaning 'illā you did.'" It is narrated from al-Akhfash, al-Kisā'ī and Abū 'Ubayda that they said: "lammā with the meaning of 'illā' is not found in the speech of the Arabs." The first: the view of some exegetes that this guardian is Allah, exalted is He. In verification: every existence other than Allah is contingent, and every contingent thing's existence is not preferred over its non-existence except by a determining cause, and this ends in the Necessary Existent in Himself. So He, glorified is He, is the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyūm) by whose guarding and sustaining existent things endure. Then He, exalted is He, explained this meaning concerning the heavens and the earth in general in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah sustains the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fāṭir: 41], and He explained it in this verse specifically concerning the human being. The reality of the speech returns to this: He, exalted is He, swore that everything other than Him is possible in existence, originated, needy, created, and nurtured. This is when we take "soul" (nafs) in the sense of the pure essence. But if we take it in the sense of the breathing soul, which is the animal soul, then it is possible that what is meant by His being a guardian of it is His being knowing of its conditions, delivering to it all its benefits, and repelling from it all its harms.

The second view: that this guardian is the angels, as He said: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [Al-An'ām: 61], and He said: ﴿On the right and on the left, a sitter. He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer ready﴾ [Qāf: 17–18], and He said: ﴿And indeed, there are over you guardians, noble writers﴾ [Al-Infiṭār: 10], and He said: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 11].

One: these guardians write down on him his deeds, both the minute and the great, until on the Day of Resurrection it comes out to him as a book which he meets, opened.

Two: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾ guards its deed, its provision and its term. When a person has completed his term and his provision, He takes it back to its Lord. Its outcome returns to the threat against the disbelievers and the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ), as in His saying: ﴿So do not be hasty concerning them. We are only counting out for them a count﴾ [Maryam: 84]. Then they will soon turn to the Hereafter, and be recompensed with what they deserve.

Three: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾, who protects it from perils and ruin, so nothing befalls it except what Allah has decreed upon it.

Four: al-Farrā' said: "Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian" guards it until he delivers it to the graves. This is the saying of al-Kalbī.

Know that when He, exalted is He, swore that for every soul there is a guardian who watches over it and records its deeds upon it, then it becomes right for everyone to strive and exert himself in attaining the most important of matters. The revealed laws and the intellects agree that the most important matters are knowledge of the Originator and knowledge of the Return, and they agree that knowledge of the Originator precedes knowledge of the Return. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, began after this with what points to the Originator.

﴿By the sky and the knocker in the night.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the knocker is?﴾ ﴿It is the piercing star.﴾ ﴿There is no soul but that it has over it a guardian.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in His Book the sky, the sun and the moon frequently, because their conditions in their forms, their courses, their risings and their settings are wondrous. As for the "ṭāriq" (knocker), it is whatever comes to you at night, whether it is a star or something else. So the ṭāriq is not in the daytime. The evidence for this is the saying of the Muslims in their supplication: "We seek refuge in Allah from the knockers of the night." It is also narrated that he (peace be upon him) "forbade a man to come to his family suddenly (ṭurūqan)." The Arabs use ṭurūq in describing a phantom (khayāl), because that state occurs mostly at night. Then, when He, exalted is He, said ﴿the knocker﴾, this was something whose hearer cannot do without knowing its intended meaning, so He said ﴿And what will make you know what the knocker is?﴾. Sufyān ibn 'Uyayna said: "Everything in the Qur'an introduced by 'what will make you know' (mā adrāka), the Messenger has informed about it; and everything in it introduced by 'what will make you know' (mā yudrīka) he has not informed about, such as His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [Ash-Shura: 17]." Then He said ﴿the piercing star﴾, meaning: it is a knocker of great affair and high rank, and it is the star by which one is guided in the darknesses of land and sea, and by which the times of rains are determined. Here are some issues:

**First issue:** The star was described as "piercing" for several reasons:

One: it pierces the darkness with its light, so it penetrates it, as it is said: "durrī" (a pearl-like star), because it repels (yadra'uhu) it, that is, pushes it away.

Two: it rises from the east penetrating the air, like something that pierces a thing.

Three: it is the one by which the devil is seen, so it pierces him, that is, penetrates him and burns him.

Four: al-Farrā' said: "the piercing star" is the star that is elevated above the stars. The Arabs say of a bird when it rises high into the belly of the sky: "it has pierced (qad thaqaba)."

**Second issue:** The star was described as a knocker because it appears at night, and you know that this is called ṭāriq; or because it knocks (yaṣukku) the jinn, that is, strikes them.

**Third issue:** Scholars differed concerning His saying ﴿the piercing star﴾. Some said: it refers to the group of grammarians, and it was said "the knocker," as it was said: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [Al-'Asr: 2]. Others said: it is a specific star. Then Ibn Zayd said: it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā). al-Farrā' said: it is Saturn (Zuhal), because with its light it pierces the thickness of seven heavens. Others said: it is the meteors with which the devils are stoned, because of His saying: ﴿So a piercing meteor pursued him﴾ [As-Saffat: 10].

**Fourth issue:** It was narrated that "Abu Ṭālib came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he regaled him with bread and milk. While he was sitting eating, a star fell, it became filled with water, then with fire. Abu Ṭālib was alarmed and said: 'What is this?' He said: 'This is a star that was thrown, and it is one of the signs of Allah.' Abu Ṭālib marveled, and the surah was revealed."

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the thing sworn by, He followed it with mention of the thing sworn to: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian.﴾ Concerning this there are issues:

**First issue:** Concerning His saying "(lammā)" there are two readings:

One: the reading of Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, Nāfi' and al-Kisā'ī, which is with the mīm lightened.

The second: the reading of 'Āṣim, Ḥamza and al-Nakha'ī, with the mīm stressed. Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī (d. 377 AH) said: "Whoever lightens it, then 'in' (inna) in his reading is the lightened form of the heavy 'inna', and the lām in 'lammā' is the one that enters with this lightened form to distinguish it from the negative 'in'; and 'mā' is a supplementary particle, like the one in His saying: ﴿So by mercy from Allah﴾ [Āl 'Imrān: 159] (and ﴿after a little﴾), and 'in' is then introduced to the oath, as it is introduced when it is heavy. As for whoever stresses it, then 'in' in his reading is the negative, like the one in His saying: ﴿In that which We had not established for you﴾ [Al-Aḥqāf: 26], and 'lammā' has the meaning of 'illā' (except/that not). He said: 'lammā' is used with the meaning of 'illā' in two places. One of them is this, and the other is in the matter of oaths: you say, 'I asked you by Allah, lammā you did such-and-such,' meaning 'illā you did.'" It is narrated from al-Akhfash, al-Kisā'ī and Abū 'Ubayda that they said: "lammā with the meaning of 'illā' is not found in the speech of the Arabs." Ibn 'Awn said: "I recited before Ibn Sīrīn 'lammā' with stress, and he denied it and said: 'Glory be to Allah, glory be to Allah!'" But al-'Utbī claimed that "lammā" has the meaning of "illā," although the light form which has the meaning of "mā" exists in the dialect of Hudhayl.

**Second issue:** The verse does not explain who this guardian is, and it also does not explain what the guardian guards the soul from. As for the first: there are two views. The first: the view of some exegetes that this guardian is Allah, exalted is He. In verification: every existence other than Allah is contingent, and every contingent thing's existence is not preferred over its non-existence except by a determining cause, and this ends in the Necessary Existent in Himself. So He, glorified is He, is the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyūm) by whose guarding and sustaining existent things endure. Then He, exalted is He, explained this meaning concerning the heavens and the earth in general in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah sustains the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fāṭir: 41], and He explained it in this verse specifically concerning the human being. The reality of the speech returns to this: He, exalted is He, swore that everything other than Him is possible in existence, originated, needy, created, and nurtured. This is when we take "soul" (nafs) in the sense of the pure essence. But if we take it in the sense of the breathing soul, which is the animal soul, then it is possible that what is meant by His being a guardian of it is His being knowing of its conditions, delivering to it all its benefits, and repelling from it all its harms.

The second view: that this guardian is the angels, as He said: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [Al-An'ām: 61], and He said: ﴿On the right and on the left, a sitter. He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer ready﴾ [Qāf: 17–18], and He said: ﴿And indeed, there are over you guardians, noble writers﴾ [Al-Infiṭār: 10], and He said: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 11].

As for the second investigation, namely: what is it that this guardian guards? There are several views:

One: these guardians write down on him his deeds, both the minute and the great, until on the Day of Resurrection it comes out to him as a book which he meets, opened.

Two: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾ guards its deed, its provision and its term. When a person has completed his term and his provision, He takes it back to its Lord. Its outcome returns to the threat against the disbelievers and the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ), as in His saying: ﴿So do not be hasty concerning them. We are only counting out for them a count﴾ [Maryam: 84]. Then they will soon turn to the Hereafter, and be recompensed with what they deserve.

Three: ﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾, who protects it from perils and ruin, so nothing befalls it except what Allah has decreed upon it.

Four: al-Farrā' said: "Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian" guards it until he delivers it to the graves. This is the saying of al-Kalbī.

Know that when He, exalted is He, swore that for every soul there is a guardian who watches over it and records its deeds upon it, then it becomes right for everyone to strive and exert himself in attaining the most important of matters. The revealed laws and the intellects agree that the most important matters are knowledge of the Originator and knowledge of the Return, and they agree that knowledge of the Originator precedes knowledge of the Return. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, began after this with what points to the Originator.

Then He said: ﴿So let man consider what he was created from.﴾ ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid.﴾ ﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs.﴾ And in this are several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-dafq* (الدَّفْقُ, pouring out) means pouring water. One says *dafaqtu al-mā'* (دَفَقْتُ الماءَ), meaning "I poured the water." The water is *madfūq* (مَدْفُوقٌ), meaning poured, and *mundafiq* (مُنْدَفِقٌ), meaning emitted. Since this water is poured out, the commentators differed about why it is described as *dāfiq* (دافِقٌ) in several ways:

First: al-Zajjāj (الزَّجّاجُ) said: its meaning is *dhū indifāq* (ذُو انْدِفاقٍ), "possessing emission," as one says *dāri'* (دارِعٌ, "armored"), *fāris* (فارِسٌ, "a horseman"), *nābil* (نابِلٌ, "an archer"), *lābin* (لابِنٌ, "a milk-possessor"), and *tāmir* (تامِرٌ, "a date-possessor"), meaning *dāri'* (one who has armor), *fāris* (one who has a horse), and so on. Al-Zajjāj mentioned that this is the view of Sībawayh (سِيبَوَيْهِ).

Second: they name the thing acted upon by the name of the actor. Al-Farrā' (الفَرّاءُ) said: the people of the Ḥijāz use this pattern more than others; they make the passive into the active when it is in the manner of an adjective, as in the saying *sirrun kātimun* (سِرٌّ كاتِمٌ, "a secret concealed"), *hammun nāṣibun* (هَمٌّ ناصِبٌ, "a worry that wearies"), and *laylun nā'imun* (لَيْلٌ نائِمٌ, "a sleeping night"), and as in His saying ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ (فِي عِيشَةٍ راضِيَةٍ), meaning *marḍiyya* (مَرْضِيَّةٍ), "pleasing."

Third: al-Khalīl (الخَلِيلُ) mentioned in the book attributed to him: *dafaqa al-mā'u dafqan wa dufūqan* (دَفَقَ الماءُ دَفْقًا ودُفُوقًا), meaning the water poured out all at once, and *indafaqa al-kūz* (انْدَفَقَ الكُوزُ), meaning the jug poured out all at once. It is said in omen-taking, when a jug or the like pours out: *dāfiqu khayr* (دافِقُ خَيْرٍ), "a gushing of good." In the book of Qutrub (قُطْرُبٍ): *dafaqa al-mā'u yadfuqu* (دَفَقَ الماءُ يَدْفُقُ) when it poured out.

Fourth: since the one possessing the emission is gushing, this description was applied to the water by way of metaphor (*majāz*).

**The second issue:** *al-ṣulb* (الصُّلْبِ) is read with two fatḥas (الصَّلَبِ) and with two ḍammas (الصُّلُبِ). There are four dialectal forms: *ṣulb* (صُلْبٌ), *ṣalab* (صَلَبٌ), *ṣulub* (صُلُبٌ), and *ṣālib* (صالِبٌ).

**The third issue:** *al-tarā'ib* (التَّرائِبُ) of the woman are the bones of her chest where the necklace rests, and each of those bones is a *tarība* (تَرِيبَةٌ). This is the view of all the lexicographers. Imru' al-Qays (امْرُؤُ القَيْسِ) said:

*Her breastbones are polished like a mirror.*

**The fourth issue:** There are two views concerning this verse. One is that the child is created from the fluid that emerges from the man's loins and the woman's breastbones. Others said that it is created from the fluid that emerges from the man's loins and his breastbones. The proponent of the second view argued for his position with two arguments:

First: the man's fluid emerges only from the loins, and the woman's fluid emerges only from the breastbones. On this assumption, no fluid emerges from between the loins and the breastbones, and that contradicts the verse.

Second: God has stated that man is created ﴿from a gushing fluid﴾, and what is described by that is the man's fluid. Then He followed it by describing it as emerging, meaning this gushing fluid emerges from between the loins and the breastbones. This indicates that the child is created from the man's fluid alone.

The proponents of the first view answered the first argument: it is permissible to say of two different things, "a great good emerges from between these two," and because the man and woman, when they unite, become like a single thing, this expression is appropriate there. They answered the second argument: this is from the figure of speech by which the name of a part is applied to the whole. Since one of the two components of the seminal fluid is gushing, this name was applied to the whole combination. Then they said: what shows that the child is created from the combined two fluids is that the man's fluid alone is small and therefore insufficient. Also, it is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When the man's fluid prevails, the child is male, and the resemblance returns to him and to his relatives; and when the woman's fluid prevails, the resemblance returns to her and to her relatives." This requires the soundness of the first view.

Know that the atheists (al-mulḥidīn, الْمُلْحِدِينَ) criticized this verse. They said: if what is meant by ﴿emerges from between the loins and the breastbones﴾ is that the seminal fluid is separated from those places, then the matter is not so; for it is only generated from the residue of the fourth digestion, and it is separated from all the parts of the body, until it takes from each limb its nature and its property, so that it becomes prepared to generate from itself similar limbs. For this reason, one who is excessive in intercourse finds weakness overtaking all his limbs. If what is meant is that most parts of the seminal fluid are generated there, this is weak; rather, most of its parts are nurtured in the brain. The evidence for this is that its form resembles the brain, and because one who frequently emits it first shows weakness in his eyes. If what is meant is that the seminal fluid's place of settling is there, this is weak; for the place of settling of the seminal fluid is the seminal vessels, which are veins intertwined with one another near the two testicles. If what is meant is that the exit of the seminal fluid is there, this is weak, for sense perception shows that this is not so.

The answer: there is no doubt that the most helpful organ in generating the seminal fluid is the brain, and the brain's successor is the spinal cord (*al-nukhā'* النُّخاعُ), which lies in the loins. It has many branches descending toward the front of the body, and these are the breastbones. For this reason God singled out these two organs for mention. Moreover, your discourse on how the seminal fluid is generated and how the limbs are generated from the seminal fluid is pure imagination and weak conjecture, while the word of God is more worthy of acceptance.

**The fifth issue:** We have explained in several places in this book that the evidence of human generation from a drop (*nuṭfa*, نُطْفَةٌ) for the existence of the Creator who chooses is among the clearest proofs, for several reasons:

The first: the wondrous compositions in the human body are more numerous, so his generation from a simple substance is more indicative of the Capable, the Chooser.

The second: a person's awareness of his own states is greater than his awareness of the states of others, so this evidence is more complete.

The third: a person's observation of these states in his children and in the children of all other animals is constant, so reasoning from it to the Chooser Creator is stronger.

The fourth: the argument from this domain, just as it definitively indicates the existence of the Chooser, the Wise Creator, likewise definitively indicates the soundness of resurrection, gathering, and raising. This is because the coming into being of man occurred through the joining of parts that had been scattered in the bodies of the two parents, indeed in the whole world. When the Creator was able to gather those scattered parts until He made from them a complete human being, it must be said that after his death and the dispersal of his parts, the Creator will certainly be able to gather those parts and make them a complete creation as they were at first. For this very reason, when God showed His evidence for the origin, He also followed it with His evidence for the soundness of the return.

If what is meant is that most parts of the seminal fluid are generated there, this is weak; rather, most of its parts are nurtured in the brain. The evidence for this is that its form resembles the brain, and because one who frequently emits it first shows weakness in his eyes. If what is meant is that the seminal fluid's place of settling is there, this is weak; for the place of settling of the seminal fluid is the seminal vessels, which are veins intertwined with one another near the two testicles. If what is meant is that the exit of the seminal fluid is there, this is weak, for sense perception shows that this is not so.

The answer: there is no doubt that the most helpful organ in generating the seminal fluid is the brain, and the brain's successor is the spinal cord (*al-nukhā'* النُّخاعُ), which lies in the loins. The second: a person's awareness of his own states is greater than his awareness of the states of others, so this evidence is more complete.

The third: a person's observation of these states in his children and in the children of all other animals is constant, so reasoning from it to the Chooser Creator is stronger.

The fourth: the argument from this domain, just as it definitively indicates the existence of the Chooser, the Wise Creator, likewise definitively indicates the soundness of resurrection, gathering, and raising. This is because the coming into being of man occurred through the joining of parts that had been scattered in the bodies of the two parents, indeed in the whole world. When the Creator was able to gather those scattered parts until He made from them a complete human being, it must be said that after his death and the dispersal of his parts, the Creator will certainly be able to gather those parts and make them a complete creation as they were at first. For this very reason, when God showed His evidence for the origin, He also followed it with His evidence for the soundness of the return.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: If I wish, I return him from old age to youth, from youth to childhood, and from childhood to the drop (nutfah).

The first issue: "Yawma" (on the day) is in the accusative, governed by "raj'ihi" (his return). But whoever makes the pronoun in "raj'ihi" refer to the water and interprets it as its return to its place of emergence from the loins and the breastbones, or to its first state, governs the time-adverb by His words "famā lahu min quwwah" (then he has no power), meaning: he has no power on that day.

The second issue: "Tubla" means "tukhtabar" (is tested). "Al-sara'ir" are what is concealed in the hearts of beliefs and intentions, and what is hidden of deeds. Regarding the manner of this testing and examination here, there are sayings:

The first: what al-Qaffal mentioned. The meaning of testing here is that the deeds of the human being on the Day of Resurrection are presented to him, and he also looks at the record which the angels wrote, containing the details of their deeds, so that he may know whether what is mentioned matches what is written. Since reckoning on the Day of Resurrection occurs in this way, it is permissible to call this meaning a trial. This designation is not far from His servants, because it is a trial and an examination, even though He is knowing of all the details of what they did and what they did not do.

The second aspect: deeds merit reward and punishment only according to their aspects. Many an act may outwardly be good while inwardly it is ugly, and sometimes the reverse. So testing them is to weigh what is considered among those conflicting aspects, through opposition and preponderance, until it becomes clear which aspect is the preponderant and which is the subordinate.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 86, verse 11–17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky, which returns [rain]﴾ ﴿and by the earth, which splits open﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ ﴿and it is not a jest﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot﴾ ﴿and I too am plotting a plot﴾ ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them a little respite﴾

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, finished with the proof of Tawhid (divine oneness) and the return (ma'ad), He swore another oath. As for His saying, ﴿By the sky, which returns﴾, we say: al-Zajjaj said, "ar-raj' (the return) is the rain, because it comes and recurs."

Know that the words of al-Zajjaj and the rest of the leading linguists are explicit that ar-raj' is not a term originally coined for rain; rather it was called raj' by way of metaphor (majaz). For the goodness of this metaphor there are several reasons:

The first: al-Qaffal said, "It is as if it derives from tarjee' al-sawt (the repetition of a sound), which is repeating it and connecting the letters with it. Likewise, rain, being something that returns time after time, was called raj'."

The second: the Arabs used to claim that the cloud carries water from the seas of the earth and then returns it (yurjiʿuhu) to the earth.

The third: they intended optimism (tafa'ul), so they named it raj' so that it would return.

The fourth: that rain returns every year.

Having understood this, we say that there are sayings among the exegetes.

The first: Ibn Abbas said: ﴿by the sky which returns﴾ means possessing rain that returns, rain after rain.

The second: the "return" of the sky is the giving of the good that comes from it, state after state, over the passage of times; it returns it, that is, gives it time and again.

The third: Ibn Zayd said: it is that it turns back and returns its sun and moon after their setting. The first saying is the correct one.

As for His saying, ﴿and by the earth, which splits open﴾, know that as-sad' (the splitting) is the cleaving, and from it is His saying: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾ [al-Rum: 43], that is, they will scatter. The exegetes have various sayings. Ibn Abbas said: it splits open for plants and trees.

Mujahid said: it refers to two mountains between which there is a crack and a passable path, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And We made in it broad roads as paths﴾ [al-Anbiya: 31]. Al-Layth said: as-sad' is the vegetation of the earth, because it splits the earth and the earth splits by it; and on this basis the plant was called sad', because it cleaves the earth.

Know that just as He, glorified, made the manner of the creation of animals a proof of knowledge of the origin and the return, in this oath He mentions the manner of the creation of plants. So the sky which returns is like the father, and the earth which splits open is like the mother, and both are among the great blessings, because the blessings of this world depend upon what descends from the sky of rain repeatedly, and upon what grows from the earth likewise. Then He, exalted, followed this oath with that which is sworn to, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, and concerning it there are issues:

First issue: concerning this pronoun there are two opinions.

The first: what al-Qaffal said, namely that the meaning is that what I have informed you of, of My power to bring you back to life on the Day when your secrets are tested, is a decisive word and a truth.

The second: that it refers to the Qur'an, that is, the Qur'an separates between truth and falsehood, as it is called al-Furqan. The first is preferable, because returning the pronoun to the previously mentioned thing is more appropriate.

Second issue: ﴿a decisive word﴾ means a judgment by which truth is separated from falsehood; from it comes fasl al-khusumat (the settling of disputes), which is ending them by ruling. It is said: "This is a decisive word," meaning one that cuts off dispute and contention. Some exegetes said: its meaning is that it is a serious truth, in accordance with His saying: ﴿and it is not a jest﴾, that is, not play. The meaning is that the Qur'an was sent down in earnest and was not sent down in play. Then He said: ﴿and it is not a jest﴾; the meaning is that the decisive clarification is sometimes mentioned in the manner of seriousness and concern for its matter, and sometimes not in the manner of seriousness; and this place is of that kind. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot﴾, and that plotting takes several forms: among them by casting doubts, such as their saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37]; ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78]; ﴿Has he made the gods one god?﴾ [Sad: 5]; ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]; ﴿It is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]. Among them by slandering it, calling it sorcery, poetry and madness. The other: that it is an adjective. If you make the modified noun explicit, it cannot be a circumstantial accusative. What is in the verse is what we mentioned in the third form, because it is permissible for it to be an adjective of the verbal noun, as if it were said: imhalan ruwaydan; and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial accusative, meaning: grant them respite without hastening.

Second issue: some said: ﴿give them a little respite﴾ extends until the Day of Resurrection, and it was diminished for this reason: He knew that everything that is to come is near. Others said: give them a little respite until the Day of Badr. The first is preferable, because what happened on the Day of Badr and in the other battles does not encompass all of them, whereas when it is taken to refer to the affair of the Hereafter it encompasses all of them. Nor is it impossible that along with that there should enter into it the affairs of this world, such as what befell them on the Day of Badr and other than it; and all of that is a warning and admonition to the people. And just as it is a warning to them, it is also an encouragement to take a path opposite to theirs in acts of obedience. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best, and may God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
